about: The Compendium's lore (bible/02-Systems/Lore.md): its categories, each a tile on the Compendium's front page with its name and a motif (client/src/game/emblemMotifs.ts), and its books, each in a category, with its name, its cover (a cloth colour and a motif) and its chapters in reading order. A chapter has its title and its text (paragraphs apart by a blank line), and is found once as `found` says: {"kind": "story"} as the story ends; {"kind": "quest", "quest": id, "task": id} as that quest's task is done; {"kind": "place", "node": id, "place": name, "bearing": degrees, "at": metres} lying at a place in a node of the world, the place named as its layout names it, "at" metres from its middle at "bearing" degrees clockwise from north. Characters keep chapters by their book's id and their own: never change an id once a chapter is played.

chapters.title: The Old Beacon
chapters.text:
The Old Beacon stands on the highest ground of the Saltgrass Downs, where the turf thins and the chalk shows through like bone. No fire has burned in it in living memory. The shepherds say their grandmothers never saw it lit, and that their grandmothers' grandmothers said the same, and that nobody up there ever thought to ask what it was built to burn.

We keep our rolls in the dry room under its stair, and our storm-glass in the racks at the top, where the wind comes in from every side at once and the whole tower hums like a struck pot. A roll is a strip of oiled linen as long as a tall man. Every caller who climbs the Beacon for the first time writes three things on it: what the weather was, what the storm did, and what it cost. Then the roll goes back into the chest, and the next caller writes below. The chest has never been empty in anyone's memory, and it has never been full.

Nobody agrees who raised the Beacon. The Downs folk say giants built it to see over the sea. The salt-wives at Shingle Landing say it was a lighthouse for a sea that once came this far inland, and they will show you shells pressed into the chalk to prove it. Our oldest roll begins with this.

> The stone was here before the storm, and the storm was here before us.

Every caller learns the first rule on these stairs. *Climb before you walk.* Lightning loves a height, and it loves whoever goes up to meet it. A caller who waits on low ground for the storm to come to them will wait their whole life, and die dry.

~

*Below, in Arlo's hand.*

You found the racks empty and the chest standing open. They took the glass, and a good many of the rolls with it. Pell's knife was stuck in the floorboards by the door, and Pell's knife does not leave his belt. Not for supper, not for sleep. Not unless he meant it to be found.

Find what they took. The rolls can wait. The glass cannot.

*Arlo Kestrel, keeper of the rolls*

chapters.title: Brineglass
chapters.text:
After a great storm the tide pools under the cliffs grow glass. It comes up out of the brine overnight, clear and square-edged as salt, and it is warm when you lift it out, warmer than any sun could make it. Some pieces hum against your palm like a bee held in a fist. The salt-wives call it *storm-tears* and sell it to travellers as charms against drowning. We call it *brineglass*, and we do not sell it.

Most of it dies within a day. The warmth goes, then the hum, and you are holding a pebble. A few pieces keep it. Those we carry up to the Beacon and set in the racks, and a held piece will keep its storm for a season or more. Turn it in your hand and you can tell which way the weather is coming by which face of it is warm.

No one has ever seen brineglass made. It is simply there after the storm, the way the tide leaves wrack. Some years there is none at all, though the storms blow as hard as ever. One roll, very old, says that after a storm with red in its lightning the pools were full of brineglass that was black, and cold, and the caller who found it carried every piece out past the rocks and gave it to the sea. She does not say why. She says it was the right thing to do, and that she did not sleep for three nights after, and that on the third night she heard it, out past the rocks, settling.

Our storm-glass, the great one, is as long as a forearm and as thick as a wrist. Every roll that mentions it names a different finder. None says it has ever gone cold.

~

The Tithe weighed it on a grain scale. We found the scale in their barns with the glass still sitting in the pan, and a chalk mark on the beam: *one tenth, owed.* Our rolls were there too, stuffed in a feed sack, unread. They had taken a tenth of everything that came out of the pools that season, and weighed our storm like a sack of barley.

That is our glass. Feel it hum. Now climb, as high as you can.

chapters.title: The First Caller
chapters.text:
Three rolls tell how the Storm came to the first of us. They are kept together, tied with the same cord, and nobody unties it but the keeper.

**The first roll** says her name was Wenna Kestrel, and that she was a shepherd on the Downs. A storm caught her flock on the high ground, and she climbed the Old Beacon to see where the sheep had run. The lightning struck the stone while she stood on it. It went into her, and it stayed. She walked down the stairs with sparks crawling in her hair, and the sheep came back to her out of the rain, every one, because they could see her from the far side of the Downs.

**The second roll** says her name was Merrow Vane, a salt-wife whose husband had drowned off the Landing. She took a piece of brineglass up onto the High Downs in the worst storm of the year and held it up to curse the sky for taking him. The storm did not strike her. It answered her. She came down with the glass still in her fist and the storm still in the glass, and she never cursed it again.

**The third roll** gives no names at all. It says two sisters stood back to back on the High Downs with one glass held up between them. The storm came down and chose one of them. The other walked to Shingle Landing the next morning, took a boat, and was not seen on Saltmere again.

The three rolls are in the same hand. The ink is the same age. The Kestrels say it is Wenna's own hand, and that she wrote the story three ways to see which the storm liked best. Others in the house say it is not Wenna's hand at all, and will not say whose it is. I have held all three up to the window, one over another, and the letters lie on each other like the same footprint walked three times.

What all three agree on is this.

*A storm. A height. Glass held up. And the storm deciding, while someone stood very still and let it.*

~

That is what you did on the High Downs. The Storm does not belong to a house. It belongs to whoever goes up to meet it and holds still while it makes up its mind. It made up its mind. It will answer now, whenever you call.

chapters.title: Quick Feet
chapters.text:
The rolls say that on the night the Storm came to the first caller, ships were seen off Shingle Landing with no lights showing. Whichever of her it was, she knew what dark ships meant. She ran.

From the Old Beacon to the Landing is most of a day's walk for a shepherd. The rolls say she got there ahead of the storm that followed her down off the Downs, and that storm was walking fast. She went through every village on the way, and at every door she knocked, whoever came out found their own feet quick under them, and ran with her. By the time the dark ships put their boats in, there was no one on the shingle to take and nothing in the houses worth carrying. The boats rowed back with their holds empty, and somebody up on the cliff laughed loud enough to be heard on the water.

We call it **Quicken**. Our grandmothers called it *the Running*. It is the Storm let into the legs instead of the hand, and it does not care whose legs they are. Call it with friends beside you and they feel it too. A caller who keeps it for themselves alone has misunderstood it.

The old callers used Grey Point Light, out on the Driftwood Moors, to carry word along the coast. A caller on the point would set the lamp-glass burning with lightning, a white so hard it hurt to look at, and the callers on the Downs would see it and run. That is how the Stormcallers held this coast before there was a town here worth holding.

So when Grey Point burns with lightning, a Stormcaller lit it. Nobody else can. When it burns and none of us lit it, one of us has been bought.

~

Pell's voice came on the wind tonight, the old way we speak across the Downs. He said *it's done*, and that I shouldn't come looking for him. Pell never could tell me no to my face. He knows I am already looking.

Let the storm into your legs. His tracks are going cold, and you will need to be quick.

chapters.title: What the Tithe Counted
chapters.text:
*Found folded in a Tithe strongbox at the camp on the Driftwood Moors. Copied here as it was written, every word, so that every caller after me can read how they think.*

> **Assessment of the Saltgrass Downs, the Driftwood Moors and the waters off them, weather held.**
>
> **Item.** Rain, falling on the Downs. Not held. Not assessed.
>
> **Item.** Wind off the sea. Not held. Not assessed.
>
> **Item.** Lightning, struck upon the high stone called the Old Beacon. Held, in glass. Assessed at one tenth of all lightning so held, from the first holding to the present, with debt and interest owed upon the arrears.
>
> **Item.** Lightning, carried in the persons of those called Stormcallers. Held. Assessed. The persons to be counted.
>
> **Item.** Persons, Stormcallers, their number. Uncounted. To be counted.
>
> **Item.** The headland called Grey Point. Longer than the chart. Under review.
>
> **Item.** The storm itself. Under review. The High Assessor writes that a thing which answers when called is a thing which is held, and a thing which is held is a thing which can be owed.
>
> *Owed since before assessment.*

That is the end of it. There is no seal and no name, only a grey wax smear where a seal should be. The hand is very neat. Whoever wrote it had written a great many of these, and had never once been made to wait for an answer.

I read the line about Grey Point three times. I have walked out to the end of that point since I was a boy. I could not tell you whether it is longer than it was. I could not tell you that it is not.

I want to burn the thing. I will not. Every caller should read how they see us. Not as people, and not as a house. As weather that somebody forgot to tax.

Their tally from the same camp names a ship carrying our lightning rods out to sea. They do not want our glass to sell. They want our rods to plant. A rod staked in the ground calls lightning down to it whether a caller is there or not. Stake enough rods in the right places and you do not need a caller at all.

They mean to take a tenth of the sky. Then they mean to take the rest.

*Arlo Kestrel*

chapters.title: No Storm on a Deck
chapters.text:
The house has an old rule. *A caller does not call the Storm from the deck of a ship.*

A ship's mast is the tallest thing for miles of open water, and lightning loves a height. Call the Storm at sea and it will come to you gladly, and it will come down the mast, and it will not stop at you. The rolls list eleven callers who broke the rule in the early days. Nine of them burned their ships to the waterline. The other two are only names. Nobody wrote down what became of them, which tells you enough.

Some callers sail anyway. They learn to call low, from the rail, with the mast at their back and a wet rope in their fist to carry the strike over the side. It takes years, and the ones who learn it do not like to talk about how they learned. If you mean to fight at sea, find one of them and buy them a drink. Don't ask about their hands.

Stranger still. The old callers who went out against Tithe ships wrote that the lightning would not take the Tithe's grey sails. The bolts struck the canvas and ran off it like rain off a gull's back, down into the sea, and the sail did not so much as smoke. Their decks burn. Their crews burn. Their sails do not. One caller cut a strip from a captured sail and brought it home. The roll says it was dry when she pulled it out of the sea, and dry every morning after, however long she left it out in the rain. Nobody in the house knows what the cloth is made from. The Tithe do not sell it, and they do not leave it behind.

~

The Tithe ship you took carried our rods wrapped in that cloth, one bundle in every hold. They knew what they were carrying and how to keep it quiet. Their crew talked, after, once they understood we were not going to ask the sea to keep them. The rods went ashore on an isle the Tithe guard.

Take a ship west, find that isle, and bring our rods home.

chapters.title: The Six Hounds
chapters.text:
When the first caller came down from the high stone, the rolls say, six lights came down the stairs with her. They were the size of apples and the blue at the root of a candle flame, and they drifted at her shoulders as if they were waiting to be told something.

On the shingle, when the dark ships' boats came in, she looked at the first man out of the surf, and one of the lights went to him. It moved faster than a gull diving. When he fell, the light did not go out. It turned in the air, and went to the next.

The callers call them *the hounds*, and we still raise six. They leave you when you send them, and they hunt whatever is nearest, and when their quarry falls they turn to another without being told. The great calling, the one you wait longest to have again, the rolls call the **Tempest**. Every caller remembers the first time they loosed it. Most remember it the way you remember the first time a horse threw you.

Sometimes a hound comes looking for a caller before the caller has called it. It drifts in off the sea, low over the water, circles the tallest thing it can find, and waits. The rolls do not say what it means. The callers who have seen it say the Storm has already decided.

Some callers raise eight. The rolls name that **Pursuit**, and say it cannot be taught, only found. It is one of the six ways.

The six ways are how a caller shapes the Storm to their own hand.

**Pursuit**, for more hounds.
**Conduction**, to make the Lash hold longer.
**Momentum**, so that Quicken sharpens your blows as well as your feet.
**Recharge**, which lets every enemy the lightning takes give a little of the Storm back.
**Overload**, which leaves the ones you Lash open to everyone else's steel.
**Gale**, which throws Quicken wider and keeps it longer.

No caller is given all six at once. You find them one by one.

~

Half our rods were here, wrapped in Tithe cloth, buried under a heap of everything else they had stolen from everyone else. Take one. Hold it while you think. The Storm in you has a shape now, and the shape is yours to choose.

chapters.title: The Lash at Weir Mill
chapters.text:
When the rolls were still short enough to read in a night, raiders came up the river road through Gullwing Vale. One caller held the narrow bridge at Weir Mill against them. Her name is smudged past reading. Every caller who has tried to make it out has read it differently, and every one of them was sure.

She did not call the Storm down from the sky. There was no time, and no height to climb. She held out her open hand and the Storm came out of it sideways, close and fast, and struck the whole front rank at once. They did not fall. They stood where they were, locked and shaking, swords still raised, while the mill wheel turned behind her and the raiders at their backs tried to shove past their own stiffened men on a bridge built for one cart.

We call it **Arc Lash**. It is the Storm with its hand open. It does not reach far, but everything in front of you feels it, and what it touches cannot move for a moment. A moment is a long time on a narrow bridge.

There is an entry further down the same roll, in a boy's careful letters.

> I want to learn the Lash. Arlo says I am too slow. I will be quick.

Under it, in the same hand but older:

> My family owes the Tithe for the boat and the boat sank. They say the tenth is due anyway.

Under that, nothing.

That boy was Pell.

I should have read that roll years ago. I keep the rolls. I never read that one so far down. I thought I knew what it said.

He lit Grey Point for the Tithe because they told him it would pay his family's tenth. He told us so at the Water Meadows, with his hands open and nothing in them. Corvane, the High Assessor, is counting the storm. Pell says he means to sell it back to us.

Come home, Pell. And you, take this. Hold out your hand, and let the Storm out sideways.

chapters.title: The Old Stones
chapters.text:
In Gullwing Vale, where the river bends below the orchards, there is a ring of standing stones the Vale folk call the Old Stones. Nobody in the Vale will graze sheep inside it, and nobody will say why, except that their grandmothers did not. The grass inside the ring grows a hand shorter than the grass outside it, and always has.

The house uses the ring to ground storms. When a storm comes in too close to the villages, a caller goes to the stones and strikes them in their order as the storm walks in, and the storm spends itself into the earth instead of into somebody's roof. *A storm grounded is spent. A storm held is owed.* That is the whole of the lesson, and most callers need twenty years to learn it.

The order is **west, then north, then east, then south**. The rolls say the storm walks in from the sea, then turns about the land the way the sun does, and you must meet it where it is going, not where it has been. Strike them out of order and you call it in without grounding it, and the Vale has a bad night.

The Tithe staked our rods round the Old Stones, one at every quarter, to pull the storm down into the ring and keep it there for Corvane. A storm that cannot spend itself does not go away. It waits. It grows. Hold one long enough and you could sell the Vale a season of lightning, or sell it the absence of one.

~

One more thing, and it is the thing that keeps me awake. Pell found it. The Old Stones are the same stone as the Old Beacon. The same grain, the same grey with green in it, the same weight in the hand. There is no quarry on Saltmere that gives that stone. There is no quarry anywhere any of us has heard of. Somebody brought it here, or somebody built both from something that was already here, and the rolls do not say which. The rolls do not even ask.

Pell laid his palm flat on the tallest stone while the rods cooled, and took it away quickly. He said it was warm. I put mine where his had been. It was cold as a grave. We have not talked about it since.

The rods are cold now. Corvane has nothing left to count.

chapters.title: Red Weather
chapters.text:
This is the page I would rather not have written. Every keeper of the rolls has felt the same, I think, because it has been written over many times, and none of them signed it.

*Some storms do not answer.*

You will know one when it comes. From far off it looks like any other: dark cloud, heavy sea. Under it, the lightning is red. The sky turns, slowly, around a point, as if it had found an axis it should not have. The cloud is lit from inside. Sometimes the rain hangs in the air for a breath before it falls. Sometimes the swell runs against the wind. Gulls sit down on the water and will not get up.

Under that sky the storm-glass goes dark in the rack. The rods hum with nothing in them. Call the Storm and nothing comes. Or something comes, and it is not the Storm, and the rolls are very short about the callers who tried to find out what.

So the rule is the oldest we have, older than climbing. *Under red weather, we come down.* We do not call. We do not count. We wait in the dry room under the stair with the glass wrapped in its cloth until the sky is the right colour again.

~

Corvane went down into the Maw of the Shallows because he believed a thing that answers no one can still be counted, and that whatever can be counted can be owed. The Vale fishermen say the Maw goes dry on the night of a red storm, the whole cove of it, down to the black rock at the bottom, and fills again at dawn as if nothing had happened. They say a great many things, the Vale fishermen. They do not fish the Maw.

He said it as he fell.

*Everything is owed. Even the storm. Even me.*

We do not know what he meant by the last of it. We have stopped asking. I have written it here because a caller should know that the Tithe have a High Assessor, and that he went looking for red weather.

Bring the storm home.

chapters.title: The Racks Are Full
chapters.text:
*Written by Pell, at Arlo's asking, so that it is on the roll in my own hand.*

I lit Grey Point for the Tithe. I set the lamp-glass burning with lightning on a clear night, which only a caller can do, and every caller on the Downs saw it and knew one of us had done it. I opened the Old Beacon to the collectors. I carried the glass down to their barns myself. They said it would pay my family's tenth. It paid one season of it. The rest is still owed, with interest, and a fee for counting it.

I thought I could sell them a little of the sky and keep the rest. You cannot sell a little of the sky. Corvane did not want a little.

I will not sell the sky again. Not for anything.

*Pell*

~

*Below, in Arlo's hand.*

The racks are full again. Pell is mending them himself, and he will not let anybody help him, and nobody has tried very hard.

The house keeps its Storm by one rule before all the rest. *Climb before you walk.* You came to us with salt still in your hair and no Art to your name, and you went up the Old Beacon before you had learned a single calling. You climbed before you walked. That is a Stormcaller.

The rolls hold one more line you should know, now that you are one of us.

On the last strip of the third roll, below its telling of the first caller and in a different ink, somebody wrote one line.

> The Storm will come back to the high stone when it is called by its name.

We have called it Storm since before anyone wrote anything down. Every keeper of the rolls has known, the way you know a thing in your teeth, that it is not its name.

Nobody has ever written its name down. Nobody in the house has ever been sure they should want to.

chapters.title: Shingle Landing
chapters.text:
*Second hour of the morning. Wind west, falling. Sea heavy.*

Every keeper of the Beacon writes in the Hours. We write the hour, the wind and the sea, and then what the light saw. Most nights the light sees nothing, and we write that too. A night when the light saw nothing is a good night, and there have never been enough of them.

A ship broke on the rocks at Shingle Landing in the first hour. A coaster out of the south, by her timbers, with a crew of eight. One came ashore alive, a boy of about twelve called Tobin. The rest the sea kept.

When the castaway I sent along the shingle found him, the first thing he asked was whether they were real. The second was that there had been lights ashore, and they had steered for them. Then rocks.

There is no light on Shingle Landing. There has not been since the old lamp there fell. A crew that knew this coast would have stood off until dawn. A crew that did not would have seen lights low on the shore, taken them for the Landing's harbour lamps, and come in.

This is how a keeper tells a false light from a true one.

**A true light** is set high and steady, and it does not move with the swell, because it stands on stone.

**A false light** is set low, on the beach or on a cart, so that from the sea it sits where a harbour ought to be. Sometimes it is swung slowly, to look like the lamp of a moored ship riding the waves. It is lit by people who want ships to come in where there is no harbour. People waiting with hooks and handcarts for whatever comes ashore.

Our Beacon should have shown that crew the rocks from miles out. It did not, because its lens was stolen nine nights ago, and without the lens its light reaches half as far as it should. The ship came in under the edge of it. I watched her come. I could not make the light go further.

That boy is the only one left who saw those lights. Keep him safe.

*Maren Hale, keeper*

chapters.title: The Barrow Field
chapters.text:
*Fifth hour of the morning. Wind west. Rain.*

Above Shingle Landing, where the Downs come down to the cliffs, there is a field of low mounds the Downs folk call the Barrow Field. Each mound is the grave of someone the sea gave back without a name. The keepers buried them there, back to the first keeper, each with a small lamp set on the mound so that whoever they were, they would not lie in the dark.

The wreckers light their false lights on our barrows. They take our lamps, the ones we set for the drowned, and use them to drown more. Then they wait on the shingle below for the ship to break, and they laugh. Tobin heard them laughing. He told me so when the castaway brought him to Ewe Fold, and then he did not say anything else for a long while.

Ewe Fold is a shepherds' steading on the high Downs, and the shepherds there have taken in the sea's children for as long as there have been Hours to record it. They ask no questions, and they keep the gate shut at night. Tobin has a bed by their fire now, and a dog that will not leave him.

~

There is a thing about the Barrow Field that every new keeper is shown, and none of us can explain.

There are forty-one barrows. The Hours record thirty-eight burials. We have counted the mounds many times, in daylight and with string, and we have read the Hours back to the first page. *Forty-one and thirty-eight.* Three of the barrows have no burial in the Hours at all, and no keeper has ever dug to find out who lies in them.

The oldest pages say we should not. They do not say why. The keeper who wrote it underlined it twice, so hard the pen went through.

Those three are not the oldest mounds, either. Every spring the grass on them comes up short and new, as if they had been closed the winter before.

Go back up to the Barrow Field tonight and put out every false light on it.

chapters.title: Aud's Lamp
chapters.text:
This is the beginning of the Divine, as the oldest Hours tell it. Three keepers wrote it down, and they do not agree on the year. They agree on everything else.

Her name was Aud, and she lived on the shingle below where the Barrow Field is now. Her husband had a boat, and one winter night he came in toward lights on the shore that should not have been there, and the boat broke on the rocks, and he did not come in at all.

Aud took a lamp down to the end of the Landing that same night and lit it, high on a post, where a true light should be. She meant to keep it burning until no boat on that coast ever steered for a false one again. She kept it lit the whole winter. She traded her nets for oil, and then her furniture, and then her husband's coat.

On the last night of the winter she had nothing left to burn. She trimmed the wick down to nothing, and the oil ran out, and she sat under the post in the dark and kept watch anyway, because she had said she would.

*The lamp did not go out.*

It burned on nothing. No oil and no wick, only a light, as steady as a candle in a shut room though the wind was blowing hard enough to lift the shingle. Aud sat under it until dawn. She never wrote down what she thought about in those hours. One telling says she sang. Another says she was talking to someone, and fell quiet whenever the light flickered, as if to listen.

At dawn a ship came in on the rocks regardless, and the drowned and the half-drowned came ashore in the surf, cold to the bone. Aud took the lamp down off its post and held it up over them. The light came out of it. It rose from the glass and hung in the air above the shingle, a small sun, and everyone under it breathed again. The cold went out of them. The water went out of their chests.

That is the **Sunwell**. Hang a sun where you stand, and everyone beneath it heals, and fights harder for it. It burns on nothing but your keeping it lit.

~

The false lights on the Barrow Field are dark now. In the wreckers' purses there was Tithe silver, paid out at Gullwing, in the Vale.

chapters.title: Burned Hands
chapters.text:
*Seventh hour of the night. Wind north, cold. Clear.*

When Aud carried her lamp up from the shingle, the Hours say, the glass of it was hot enough to burn, though there was nothing in it burning. She would not put it down. By the time she reached the first cottage her hands were blistered to the wrist.

She set the lamp on a table and, without thinking, the way you would hold your hands to a fire, held them in its light. The blisters closed. The skin came back. The Hours say it came back from the inside out, as if the light remembered the shape her hands ought to be and simply put them back that way.

Every keeper is taught to say it the same way. *The light remembers you whole.* Some keepers say it remembers better than we do. They do not say it loudly.

We call it **Mend**. It is the Divine turned inward, on the keeper and not on the ones she keeps, and it comes quick. There are keepers who think it selfish and never use it. The Hours think otherwise. A keeper who will not mend herself will be dead by her third winter, and then who keeps the lamps?

Aud had a word for when the light spills over, when a keeper mends herself and those standing near her mend a little too. She called it **Mercy**. It is one of the six graces, and you will find it, or it will find you.

~

The Tithe beat the people of Gullwing for seeing the wreckers paid there. They beat the miller's son with a cart-whip in front of his mother, and told the village that the next time it saw anything, it would see nothing ever again. The Vale folk are frightened, and they are angry, and they have sent word that the Tithe are coming back.

They will be back. Hold Gullwing, and keep the wounded alive while you do it, and the light will keep you alive while you keep them.

chapters.title: Gullwing
chapters.text:
*Third hour of the afternoon. Wind south. Smoke from the Vale.*

Ask in Gullwing why the village carries that name, and you will be told it is for the gulls that nest in the barn roofs, though Gullwing is a long way from the sea and the gulls should not be there. Ask a keeper, and you will be told a different story, which you will read in these Hours soon enough.

Over the door of Gullwing's oldest barn hangs a keeper's lamp-hook, worn thin as a reed. The first page of the Hours that names Gullwing at all calls it a new village.

Gullwing has kept our wounded since before Overlook had a wall. When the wreckers' wars were at their worst, on this coast and down the Vale, the keepers brought the hurt up the river road to Gullwing, and the Vale folk took them into their barns and their beds and did not ask whose side they had been on. Some of those wounded were wreckers. Gullwing nursed them too. When they were well they were walked to the Vale's edge and told never to come back, and most of them never did.

Every keeper learns this at Gullwing. *A keeper does not stand in front of the wounded to be brave. A keeper stands in front of the wounded because that is where the light reaches furthest.* Hang the Sunwell over the ones who need it most, and stand under it with them.

You held Gullwing. The miller's son lived. His mother asked me to write that down in the Hours, so that every keeper after me would read it. I have written it. *He lived.*

~

The wreckers' ship waits offshore for its pay. The Tithe pay their wreckers in grey coin. Since Gullwing saw, they pay them at sea, where nobody can watch it change hands. Sail west and find that ship.

chapters.title: Wreckers' Silver
chapters.text:
*Ninth hour of the night. Wind west, rising. Sea rough.*

Found aboard the wreckers' ship, a purse of Tithe silver. Here is what the Hours know of it.

The Tithe pay in their own coin, a thin grey disc a little wider than a thumb. It is called silver, though it is not silver, and it is not lead, and no smith in Overlook will say what it is. There is no face on it. There is no mark of any port or any king. One side is smooth, and the other is cut with a single straight line, edge to edge, like a sum that has been ruled off. Merchants in Overlook will not take it, and the Tithe do not care, because the Tithe do not spend it in Overlook. They spend it on the shingle, on the Moors, in the cabins of ships like this one. It buys lights in the wrong places.

The wreckers' captain told our castaway, after the fight, that the Tithe pay a tenth of every wreck they cause. A tenth of the cargo. The Tithe keep the rest. He did not seem to find this strange. *Everybody pays the Tithe a tenth*, he said. *We're the only ones they pay it back to.*

He also said there was a cove where his crew buried what they could not sell. He said it to save his neck, and it did.

~

The keepers have an old rule about wreckers. We do not hang them. We do not burn their boats, though we could. *We put out their lights, every one, and we leave them in the dark.* It is worse than hanging. A wrecker in the dark is only a man on a cold beach, waiting for a ship that is not going to come. Most of them find other work within the year. The ones who do not are usually found by the sea.

This captain will be put ashore at the Vale's edge, the way Gullwing does it, and told not to come back. Whether he comes back is his own business.

He bought his neck with a cove. Whatever they took is buried there.

chapters.title: What the Sea Gives Back
chapters.text:
*Fourth hour of the morning. Wind light. Fog in the cove.*

The keepers keep a list. It is the longest thing in the Hours. Every wreck we have ever seen, every name we were able to learn, and against each one, what came ashore and where it went. A keeper does not keep what the sea gives back. A keeper finds out whose it was and gives it to their kin, and if there are no kin, it goes into the Beacon's store for the next family that loses a boat. That is the rule. It has always been the rule.

The wreckers' cove held twenty years of other people's lives. Sea chests, wedding rings, a child's wooden horse with the paint worn off, a ship's bell. Every one of them will go on the list, and the list will go to the kin. It will take me all winter. I am glad of the work.

The bell troubles me. It is cast with a ship's name, and that name is on our list. The list says she went down off Grey Point with all hands, in a winter it gives as eleven years before the first keeper was born. The bell is bright. There is not a speck of green on it.

*The lens was not there.*

I should write here what the Hours say about the lens, because the castaway will want to know, and because I would rather they read it from me than hear it in the plaza.

The Beacon's lens was not made. Nobody ever ground it. It was brought up. The Hours give three tellings of how.

**In the first**, a fisherman dragged it up from the deep water off Grey Point in his net, and it was so heavy it nearly sank him.

**In the second**, a keeper carried it out of a tomb in the cliffs whose door she never found again.

**In the third**, it simply washed up on Shingle Landing the morning after the worst storm in the Hours, lying on the stones in the sunrise, bright and dry, as if it had been set down there.

In all three it is the only glass on this coast a lamp burning on nothing will shine through properly. Every other glass dims the Divine. That one makes it reach.

~

Their hoard, but not our lens. Choose what the light becomes in your hands. There are six graces, each named by the keeper who first found it: **Radiance**, **Mercy**, **Wings**, **Zeal**, **Searing** and **Resolve**.

chapters.title: The Gull of Fire
chapters.text:
*First hour of the morning. Wind east. The Hulks burning.*

This is the last of Aud's story, as the Hours tell it, and the strangest part.

On the dawn after the night Aud's lamp burned on nothing, when the drowned had breathed again under her small sun, the wreckers came down the shingle with their hooks and handcarts, the way they always had. They had not counted on anyone being alive. They had certainly not counted on Aud.

She stood up with the lamp in her hands, and something rose out of it. The Hours say it was a gull, or the shape of one, made all of fire, as bright as the sun coming up behind it. It flew low and fast along the shingle, and everywhere its shadow passed, the wreckers' boats drawn up on the beach caught and burned. Then it turned at the end of the Landing, came back along the same line, and went into the lamp again as if into a nest.

The fishermen of the Vale saw it from twenty miles off, a bird of fire going over the shoulder of the Downs at dawn. They named the place they stood in for it. That is how Gullwing has its name, and why the gulls still nest in its barns so far from the sea.

We call it **Dawnflare**. It burns the dark away, and everything standing in the dark with it. Some keepers can send it back along its line for a second pass, as Aud's gull came back to her. The Hours call that **Wings**.

~

The Saltbreaker Hulks are old ships dragged up onto the Moors long ago and made into houses. Nobody remembers who dragged them there, or how, for they lie a mile inland, and their keels are crusted with barnacles that only grow below the tide. The Reeve who kept them bought our lens from the wreckers and sold it on. He told our castaway the Tithe had bought it fairly, and to go home.

*Nothing stolen is bought fair.*

chapters.title: Red, White, Green, Gold
chapters.text:
*Tenth hour of the night. Wind north-west. Grey Point lit wrong.*

Every lamp on this coast that a keeper tends shows one of four lights, and every sailor who knows these waters knows them by heart: **red, white, green and gold**.

**Red** is for rocks. Where you see red there is something under the water that will open your hull, and you keep it on your left hand and stand off.

**White** is for the way. It shows the deep channel, the line a ship can follow safely in the dark.

**Green** is for harbour. It means there are people ashore who will take your lines and give you a fire.

**Gold** is for home. On this coast gold means only one thing. It means the Beacon at Overlook, and that you are almost there.

~

Grey Point Light stands at the end of the point that runs out from the Driftwood Moors. It is older than the Beacon by most tellings, and it alone shows all four, through a turning shade, in their order: red, then white, then green, then gold. The Tithe have been showing them in the wrong order, white over the rocks and gold over nothing, calling ships onto the point and taking them there.

On the night Grey Point first burned for the Tithe, the keeper on watch here wrote that its light was not lamp-light at all. It was the colour of a storm. She wrote that she had never seen a light like it. Then she wrote, underneath, that she had, once, as a girl, out on the Downs, and that she would ask the Stormcallers about it in the morning.

She asked. Arlo Kestrel told her that before that night, Grey Point had not burned with lightning in his lifetime, nor in his mother's. She is sure of what she saw as a girl. So, I think, is he. Neither of them is a liar, and I have stopped trying to make the Hours agree with themselves.

The castaway set the shade turning in its right order tonight, red, white, green and gold, and Grey Point burns true. And when its gold came round and fell on the cliffs beneath the point, it lit a door in the rock that no keeper living has ever found.

*The door is the colour of the inside of a shell.*

chapters.title: The Pearl Tomb
chapters.text:
*The hour unknown. No wind. The light does not change.*

The castaway spoke this to me through the lamps, from the door of the Pearl Tomb, and I have written it as they said it.

The walls are lined with something like the inside of a shell, pale and shining, smooth as glass, and they go back into the cliff much further than they should. They paced the cliff above it afterwards. The Tomb is longer than the headland it is cut into.

There are lamps everywhere. On every ledge, in every niche, hanging from the roof on chains that run up into the dark. Hundreds of them. All of them are lit.

*None of them is burning anything.*

There is no oil in them. There are no wicks. They put a hand to one, very carefully, and the glass was cool. It is Aud's light, the light that burns on nothing but its keeping, in more lamps than every keeper in the Hours has ever tended together. Somebody kept them. Somebody is still keeping them, or was until very recently. There is no dust on the ledges.

There is no body in the Pearl Tomb. They searched. It is called a tomb because the old tellings call it one, and because the shape of it is a tomb's: a long room, and at the end of it a raised stone slab, empty. Our lens was standing on the slab, wrapped in grey Tithe cloth, as if somebody had laid it out to be mourned.

The Reeve answered to someone in there. Our castaway found them, and fought them, and ended it, and never saw their face. Before they fell they said one thing.

*The Tithe will light its own lamps.*

I think they meant it as a threat. I am not sure, now, that it was one.

~

There is a page missing from the oldest Hours. I have always known it was there, because the stub is still sewn into the binding, and the next page begins in the middle of a sentence about a door in the cliffs. The tear is very old. I had always thought someone tore it out by accident.

I no longer think so. I looked at the stub again tonight, under a lamp that burns on nothing. It was cut, clean along a ruled line, edge to edge, as straight as the line on a grey coin.

Then they will burn without us. Bring the lens home.

chapters.title: The Beacon Lit
chapters.text:
*First hour of the night. Wind west. Clear. The Beacon lit.*

The lens is back in the Beacon. The light goes out over the Pale Expanse as far as it ever did, and further, the watch thinks, though a watch always thinks that on the first night. Every ship at sea will see it. Tobin watched it light from the top of the Downs at Ewe Fold, with the dog beside him. He waved. From the Beacon I could not see him wave, but I am told that he did, and I believe it.

You will have heard it said in Overlook that if you ask three people who built the Beacon, you will hear four names. That comes from the Hours. The first page of the Beacon's own Hours names four keepers who lit it first, and it does not say which of them came first, or why there are four.

The first is **Aud of the Shingle**, which cannot be right, because Aud lived and died at the Landing before there was a Beacon to light.

The second is **Corran Hale**. He is my grandmother's grandmother's grandfather, if the family is to be believed, and the family is not to be believed about much.

The third is written only as **the brothers Penhallow**, which is two names, but the page counts it as one.

The fourth is written as **the stranger who came ashore**.

That is all it says. There is no name. Every keeper who has read that line has wondered about it, and some have gone looking, and none of us has found anything more. The ink of that line is darker than the rest of the page. For forty years I have told myself it was gone over later, by some keeper with a heavy hand. I have never been able to see where.

*The light was never ours.* Aud did not make it. She only kept it burning when there was nothing left to burn, and it stayed. We are not its owners. We are only the people who would not let it go out.

~

You walked the shingle. You kept a boy alive. You put out the false lights and carried the true one into the Vale, and you held it over the wounded while the Tithe came at you. You set Grey Point true. You went into the Pearl Tomb and you came out again.

You light the way now. Write it in the Hours: the hour, the wind, the sea, and then what the light saw. The rest will come.

*Maren Hale, keeper*

chapters.title: How to Follow
chapters.text:
*Every page of this book is written in the margins of a page we took from the Tithe. Their sums run down the middle. Ours run round the edge. Nobody signs a page. If you are reading it, you are meant to.*

**How to follow a collector.**

**Never close.** Close is how you are seen. Keep him at the distance where you could lose him, and do not lose him. If you are near enough to hear him breathe, you are a fool, and he is hearing you.

**Do not watch him.** Watch what he watches. A collector looks at doors, at livestock, at the depth of a cart's ruts, at whether a chimney is smoking. He is counting. Watch what he counts and you will always know where he is going next, and you can be there before him with your back turned.

**Walk as if you have somewhere to be.** Nobody on the Downs is ever only walking. Carry something. A basket is good. A dead hare is better.

**When he stops and turns, do not stop.** Do not turn. Walk past him, wish him good day, and go round the next wall. He will forget you before he has finished turning back.

**He will feel you, sometimes.** Collectors have a sense for being followed, the way a ewe has a sense for weather. When he feels you, let him. Let him settle. Then begin again. The worst thing you can do is be the thing he felt.

~

Who are the collectors? Mostly, people from the Downs. They collect from their neighbours, and their neighbours know them, and pour them a cup of something when they call, and pay. That is how the Tithe works. It is never far away. It does not come over the sea under grey sails, not at first. It comes from the farm next to yours, with a tally in its coat.

Ask a collector how long he has worked for the Tithe and he will tell you, every time, that he started this year. Ask his neighbours, and they will tell you he has collected from them since they were children. Both believe it.

This one left his tallies in the ruin at the Chalkpit while he went to eat. Lift every one before he comes back.

chapters.title: Tallies
chapters.text:
A Tithe tally is a strip of something thin and pale, a hand long, that is not bone and is not wood. It does not burn well. It does not rot. Down one edge are notches, and the notches are a sum. Down the other a name is burned, small and neat, in the Tithe's hand.

*A tally does not record what you owe. It records what the book says you owe.* These are not the same thing, and every Veiled learns the difference before anything else.

You can pay what you owe. Many on the Downs do. They pay the tenth of their wool and their grain and their lambs, and the collector cuts a notch from the tally, and the sum is less. But the tally is only ever a copy. The sum on it is copied from the book. And the book does not get smaller when you pay.

There were nineteen tallies in the ruin, in three bundles. Every one had a different sum on it. Every one had the same name.

*It was yours.*

You washed ashore on Saltmere with nothing but the clothes the sea left you. The Tithe had already written your name nineteen times, with nineteen different sums against it, on the tallies of a collector who works the Downs. That means they knew you would come ashore on Saltmere before the sea did. It means the page with your name on it was written before your ship broke.

We have seen this before. Not often. Enough to know what it looks like.

That is why I want your page. Not for you, though you will be glad of it. For us. A page written before its person comes is a page that came from somewhere, and we would very much like to know where.

Three bundles, nineteen tallies, and your name on every one. The book is close.

chapters.title: The First Page Burned
chapters.text:
The oldest margin in this book tells how the Shadow came to the first of us. It is written round the edge of a Tithe page so old its sums have faded to nothing. The margin has not faded at all.

The first of us has no name in this book. That is the point of her. Some margins call her a woman and some call him a man, and we keep both, because the margins were written by people who loved them and we will not choose between them. This margin says she.

Her name was in their book, the margin says, and the sum against it was more than a life could pay. So she went to the reckoner who kept that book, in the dark, the way you went into the Chalk Adit today: unseen, alone, and with nothing in her hands. She found her page. She did not read it. She tore it out and held it in a candle until it was ash.

The smoke from the page did not rise. It gathered. It drew in on itself in the air above the candle, darker than the room was dark, until it was the size and the shape of a raven. It sat on her shoulder. It looked at her, the margin says, as if it knew her very well.

When the reckoner's guards came through the door, the raven went to them. It struck, and struck, and every wound it gave them closed one of hers. She walked out past them with the bird on her shoulder, and nobody laid a hand on her.

The reckoner never looked up from his table. He went on copying while she burned the page, and while his guards fell, and while she walked out. The margin says that when she looked back from the door his pen was writing her name again, very slowly, as if he could not remember how it was spelled.

We call it the **Duskraven**. Every Veiled learns to call it, and it is never quite the same bird twice. It eats what was written about you, the margins say, and gives it back to you as breath. The ones it wounds take more harm from everything after. The one it belongs to is healed by every wound it gives.

~

You came unseen. Good. The reckoner has gone to Moorhold, on the Moors. Take the dark with you. Its raven wounds them, and heals you.

chapters.title: The Dark Between Stars
chapters.text:
Ask a sailor on the Pale Expanse how to steer by night and he will tell you about the stars. Ask an old one, one who has been out past where the charts agree with each other, and he may tell you about the dark between them instead.

The old sailors say the dark between the stars is not empty. They say it is cold, colder than any winter, and sharp, the way the edge of new ice is sharp. They say that sometimes, on very clear nights far out, you can feel it looking back at you, and that if you hold still enough, it stops.

*The Veiled learned to throw it.*

The margin that tells this is short. It says only that the second of us went out onto the Moors on a clear night with no moon, lay down in the heather, and looked up until the stars went out one by one and only the dark between them was left. When she came back to Overlook in the morning there was frost on her hands, though it was high summer, and she could throw it.

The margin does not say how many of the stars came back. Our sailors have counted, on clear nights off the Moors, and come back with different numbers.

We call them **Dusk Daggers**. Hold them, aim them, let them go, and they fall where you look and whirl there, cold as the gap they came from, cutting everything that stands in them. What they cut is marked, the way the book marks a name. Every blade that strikes it after, yours and your friends', strikes deeper.

The daggers come with one warning, and here it is. *When you throw them, do not look at the dark they are made of. Look at where they will fall. The dark does not mind being used. It minds being looked at.*

~

His guards hold Moorhold, too many to walk past. So do not walk. Throw.

chapters.title: Moorhold
chapters.text:
Moorhold stands on the high ground in the middle of the Driftwood Moors, a square stone keep with a ditch round it that is always full of black water, even in a dry year. It is older than the Tithe. Nobody on the Moors knows who built it, or for what, and those who say they know all say something different.

The Tithe made it a counting-house.

This is what we found inside, for the book.

**Twelve rooms.** In every room a table and a chair, and every chair faces the wall. Not the door, not the window. The wall. On the tables, paper, ink and sand, and nothing else at all. No food. No cups. No beds anywhere in the keep, though the guards say the reckoners sometimes stay a month.

**In the deepest room**, a shelf of tallies, thousands of them, each notched and named. We did not have time to read them all. We read enough. There are names on that shelf for people who live on the Moors. There are names for people in Gullwing, and in Overlook, and in Sunspire and Rimeholt. There are names for people in ports that are ruins now, whose people are gone. Their sums are still going up.

**On the wall** facing one of the chairs, somebody had scratched a single line with a fingernail, over and over, until the plaster was worn through to the stone. A line straight across, edge to edge. It is the same line that is cut into every grey coin the Tithe pays out. It is the line a reckoner draws under a sum, to say the sum is finished.

We do not know whose chair it was. We do not know what they had finished.

~

The reckoner was not here. He put to sea with the book, aboard a Tithe ship, two days before you came. He knew you were coming. He has read your page.

chapters.title: Tally Ships
chapters.text:
Most Tithe ships carry cannon and crews and the tenth of somebody's cargo. Some carry nothing but paper. We call those the *tally ships*, and they are the ones worth taking.

A tally ship is never in a hurry. It goes from counting-house to counting-house along the coasts of the Pale Expanse, slowly, and at every one it takes on paper and puts off paper. It never stays in a port overnight. It flies no flag. Its sails are grey and plain, and the Stormcallers will tell you, if you ask, that lightning will not take them.

The crews of tally ships do not speak to one another. We have watched them through glasses for days at a time, and they work the ship well and fast and in silence, the way a hand works without talking to its fingers. When they are boarded they fight in the same silence. When they are beaten they do not beg.

There was no book aboard the ship you took. There was a log, kept in an ordinary hand, which is rare enough that we kept it. It records weather, and headings, and the names of the counting-houses where the ship called. Most of the names we know. Three we do not. They are written as plainly as the rest, with bearings and distances from known headlands, and when we lay those bearings on our charts, they point at open sea.

Wren says they are mistakes. Wren is usually right. Wren also took our oldest chart down from the wall that night and sat up with it until morning, and she has not said why.

~

The log names the reckoner's isle. He went ashore there with his ledger and his guards, and he is waiting for you, because he has read your page and he knows you are coming. Go anyway. That is one thing the book has never understood about us. *Knowing we are coming has never once stopped us coming.*

chapters.title: The Reckoner's Ledger
chapters.text:
*No book on the isle. Only his ledger, in a cipher.*

The reckoner's ledger is a small thing, black-bound, the size of a hand. Every page inside is ruled into four columns, and every column is full of a cipher that is not letters and is not numbers. It is the same cipher the Tithe use in every counting-house from here to Rimeholt, and almost no one alive can read it. Wren can. Wren will not say how she learned.

Before you go to her, I will tell you about the six habits, because you will need them, and because the dark in your hands is waiting for you to choose what it becomes.

Every Veiled shapes the Shadow by habits. They are not taught. They are caught, the way you catch a way of walking from someone you follow for long enough. There are six, and these are their names.

**Hunger**, in which the raven gives back all it takes, and not half.
**Night**, which lets the margin keep you longer.
**Blades**, which throws the daggers wider and lets them whirl longer.
**Hunt**, in which a blade struck from the margin gives back half the waiting.
**Dread**, in which every kill the dark makes on a marked enemy keeps the raven longer at your shoulder.
And **Cruelty**, which cuts deepest where the dark has marked, and which the Veiled who have it do not talk about.

No one catches all six at once.

Choose what the dark becomes in your hands.

~

Take the ledger to Wren at Vale Mouth. Meet her there, follow her, and keep quiet. She will tell you what it says when she has finished reading it, and not before. In all the years I have known her, Wren has never told anyone anything before she had finished.

chapters.title: The Margin
chapters.text:
Wren has read the ledger.

Here is your entry, as she gave it to me. I have put it into plain words, and I have left nothing out.

> **Washed ashore, Saltmere.** One life, assessed.
> **Owed:** the tenth of it, with debt, interest and the fee.
> **Paid:** half. Paid by a hand in Overlook.
> **Remainder owing.**

Somebody in Overlook has paid half of what the Tithe say you owe. They did it before you came ashore, because the entry was written before you came ashore. They did it without telling you, and without telling us, and we know where every grey coin in Overlook goes. Or we thought we did.

*Interesting.*

~

Now, the margin.

Every page of the Tithe's book has a margin, as every page has. Nothing is ever written in it. The book writes everything, the names and the sums and the ports and the ships and the weather, and it never writes in the margins. We do not know why. We think perhaps it cannot.

The first of us learned to step into the margin. Not to hide. To be, for a breath or two, in the one place on the page where nothing is written. A Veiled who steps into the margin drops and rolls and is gone between one heartbeat and the next. No eye finds them, because there is nothing there to find. Strike from the margin and you come back onto the page at once, with your blade already in something, and a blade struck from the margin always finds the part that matters.

We call it **Vanish**. You walked the orchard with Wren while the collectors worked the trees around you, heads down, and not one of them looked up. That was the first lesson. The coven gave you the rest.

*You're the one Thule couldn't drown*, Wren says. Captain Brannoc Thule threw you off a burning deck into the sea in a storm, and the sea gave you back. Beside your entry in the ledger is a column she cannot read. It is the only column in the whole ledger she has never been able to read. She says it is nearly the Tithe's cipher. Close, the way a child's copy of a letter is close.

Vanish now, and follow the book.

chapters.title: Tithe, Debt, Interest, Fee
chapters.text:
*Written round a page of the reckoner's own sums, found beside his chest at Valeguard.*

The Tithe count in four, and always in the same order.

**First, the tithe.** A tenth of everything. A tenth of the cargo, the harvest, the lambs, the catch. A tenth of the lightning in a Stormcaller's glass. A tenth of a life, if it comes to that, and it does.

**Second, the debt.** The debt is what you owe for not having paid the tithe. It is charged the moment the tithe is due, whether you have had the chance to pay or not. Nobody on the Pale Expanse has ever been out of debt to the Tithe, because the debt is counted before the tithe is collected.

**Third, the interest.** The interest is what the debt grows by while you are paying it. It is always a little more than anyone can pay.

**Fourth, the fee.** The fee is what it costs to be written down. It is charged for the ink. You pay the Tithe for the honour of having your name in their book, and the fee is added to the debt, and the debt grows its interest, and the tithe is taken again next season from whatever is left.

The reckoner's chest opened to those four marks, touched in that order, because that is the order he counts in, and a reckoner counts in no other.

~

There is something you should understand about us, now that you are close to being one of us. *The Veiled do not pay the fee.* We cannot be charged for what is not written. Once your page is burned, the fee has nothing to fall on. The debt has nothing to grow from. The tithe comes looking, and finds a margin.

The chest was empty but for a slip of Tithe paper in the reckoner's hand, the pen pressed so hard it had torn the paper. One word:

> Grotto.

chapters.title: The Book's Keeper
chapters.text:
Kraken's Grotto opens at the bottom of the cliffs, where the sea goes in and does not come back out. The fishermen say it eats boats. The Tithe say it keeps the book. They are describing the same thing.

The book's keeper never leaves the Grotto. We have watched the entrance for longer than anyone in the house has been alive, in turns, from the rocks, and we have never once seen the keeper come out. Food goes in, sometimes, on Tithe boats. Now and then a reckoner comes for the book and carries it off for a season, to copy from, and always brings it back. The reckoner you followed was taking it home.

What we know of the book, we know from the margins of its copies, and from what reckoners say when they think nobody is listening. Here it is, all of it.

**No reckoner writes in the book.** They only copy from it. Every tally, every ledger, every assessment on every counting-house table is copied out from the book by a reckoner sitting with his back to the door, and the book is never written in, and the book is never short of pages.

**The ink in the book is always wet.** A reckoner who touches a page comes away with ink on his fingers, however old the page.

**The book has pages for places that are not on any chart.** It has pages for ports that were burning long before the Tithe had ships to burn them with. It has names in it for people who have not yet washed ashore.

Before the keeper fell, he said one thing to you.

*Your name stays written. The book remembers.*

~

Wren says she found your page, that your name is on it, and that she read no further. I believe her. Wren has never read further than she meant to in her life.

She says the book, or the part of it the keeper kept, which may not be the same thing, is heavier than a book should be. It is warm. Every time she set it down on the rock it fell open at your page. She shut it and put a stone on it, and turned to the water to wash the ink off her hands. When she turned back, it lay open at your page, and the stone was in the sea.

Bring it to me.

chapters.title: Unwritten
chapters.text:
*Written in the last margin, round a page that is no longer there.*

I burned your page unread. I want you to know that. I did not read your name, or the sum against it, or anything else the book had to say about you. Wren read your name and stopped there. Nobody else in this house has seen it.

The smoke did not rise. It gathered, as it always does, and sat on my wrist for a breath, and looked at me as if it knew me, and then it went where it goes.

*The Tithe will have to remember you unwritten.*

This is what we are. You will hear it said in Overlook that the Veiled hide, that we keep to the dark, that we are the Shadow because we like the night. None of it is true, and none of it is worth correcting. *We are not hidden. We are unwritten.* The Shadow is the space where the book cannot reach: the margin, the dark between stars, the place where a burned page used to be. It is the one thing in the whole of the Pale Expanse that nobody has a tally for.

Every Veiled has had a page burned. Most burned their own. A few, the ones the house remembers longest, have burned somebody else's, for nothing, and never told them.

Somebody in Overlook paid half of your debt before you came ashore. Somebody's hand was in that ledger before yours was. The book was waiting for you with your name already written, and the sea gave you back to us when Thule meant it to keep you.

Who paid half? That question keeps, and so do we.

~

*Below, in Wren's hand.*

We never say welcome. You will know it anyway.
